narrative:
The model predicted a 72.3% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and also worked against you; you again finished in the bottom decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile.

Your LSAT score was the second most important piece of information, and it worked in your favor. At 39, you scored above the average of accepted applicants. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not enough to overcome the two weak academic-rank signals.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing as a clearer indicator of future bar-exam difficulty than your solid LSAT performance.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your class rank in the remaining years, seek academic support early, and consider retaking the LSAT only if you can reach a significantly higher score. Once you have stronger evidence of consistent academic performance, you will be in a much better position to reapply.
